history.heading: A fortress city
paragraphs: In 963 Count Siegfried acquired a rocky promontory and built a castle, the origin of the city of Luxembourg. The County, later Duchy, of Luxembourg became powerful; in the 14th and 15th centuries the House of Luxembourg produced several Holy Roman Emperors and Kings of Bohemia.
Luxembourg's fortifications, called the "Gibraltar of the North", were contested by Burgundy, Spain, France, Austria and Prussia over centuries; their remains are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: In 1815 Luxembourg became a Grand Duchy in personal union with the King of the Netherlands. It lost more than half its territory to Belgium in 1839. The 1867 Treaty of London declared it permanently neutral, and the fortress was dismantled. The personal union with the Netherlands ended in 1890, and a branch of the House of Nassau became the grand ducal family.

Germany occupied Luxembourg in both world wars, and many Luxembourgers resisted. After 1945 Luxembourg abandoned neutrality and became a founding member of NATO, the Benelux and the European communities.

culture.heading: Multilingual society
paragraphs: Luxembourg has three administrative languages: Luxembourgish, the national language, French and German. Most residents speak several languages. Nearly half the population is foreign, with large Portuguese, French, Italian and Belgian communities. Most people are Catholic by tradition.
The national day, 23 June, celebrates the Grand Duke's official birthday. Judd mat Gaardebounen (smoked pork with broad beans) is a national dish, and Moselle wines are produced locally.

politics.heading: Constitutional monarchy
paragraphs: Luxembourg is a parliamentary democracy and the world's only remaining grand duchy. Grand Duke Henri reigned from 2000 until he passed the throne to his son Guillaume in October 2025. The Chamber of Deputies is elected, and the prime minister leads the government.
Luxembourg is home to EU institutions, including the Court of Justice of the EU, the European Investment Bank and the European Court of Auditors.

economy.heading: A wealthy financial centre
paragraphs: Luxembourg has one of the highest GDPs per person in the world. It is a leading international financial centre, especially for investment funds, and also hosts satellite company SES and the European headquarters of many tech firms. Steel, once dominant through Arbed (now ArcelorMittal, headquartered there), shaped its development.
About half of the workforce commutes daily from France, Belgium and Germany. Public transport is free nationwide. The currency is the euro.
